name: Tenses
summary: Past simple, present perfect and time phrases, including Task 1.

paragraphs: Tense tells the reader when something happens: in the past, now or in the future, and whether it is finished or still connected to the present. In conversation, people often understand each other even when the tense is wrong, because the listener can ask a question. In writing, the reader cannot ask, so the tense has to do that job.

For IELTS, you do not need all twelve English tenses. A small group does almost all the work: the present simple, the past simple, the present perfect, the past perfect and a few future forms. This page focuses on choosing between them, which is where most mistakes happen.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Finished past time → past simple. Past up to now → present perfect. Facts and descriptions → present simple.

paragraphs: Tense errors are easy for examiners to spot, because time words such as in 2010, since 2015 and by the end of the period make the correct tense obvious. When the tense does not match the time word, the reader notices immediately.

In Task 1, the tense depends on the dates in the visual. In Task 2, it depends on whether you are describing a general truth, a recent change or a past event. Getting this right is one of the quickest ways to make your writing look controlled.
Before the rules, here is the small toolkit you will use. Each tense has one main job. Most errors happen when a learner chooses a tense by feel rather than by its job.

rows: finished actions at a stated past time
from the past up to now
By the time the factory closed, most workers had left.
will / is expected to + base verb
The figure is expected to reach 50% by 2030.

sections.title: Rule 1: Past simple for finished time
sections.label: Rule 1: Past simple for finished time

paragraphs: When a sentence includes a finished time, such as in 2010, last year, ten years ago or in the 1990s, the action is complete and fixed in the past. English uses the past simple for this, and the present perfect is not possible.
This is the most important tense rule for Task 1, because almost every past date in a chart calls for the past simple.

rows: The bridge opened ten years ago.
Few homes had internet access in the 1990s.

items.text: In 2010, the number of visitors has increased.
In 2010, the number of visitors increased.
Ten years ago, few people have owned smartphones.
Ten years ago, few people owned smartphones.

sections.title: Rule 2: Present perfect for the past up to now
sections.label: Rule 2: Present perfect for the past up to now

paragraphs: The present perfect connects the past with the present. Use it when something started in the past and continues now, or when a past change still matters now and no finished time is mentioned.
Two words are strong signals: since (a starting point) and for (a length of time up to now). Phrases such as recently, so far and in recent years point the same way.

rows: She has lived here for ten years.
Online shopping has grown in recent years.
The government has not acted yet.

items.text: Since 2015, house prices rose sharply.
Since 2015, house prices have risen sharply.

blocks.title: Quick test
blocks.text: If you can add a finished date (in 2010, ago), use the past simple. If you cannot, and the effect still matters now, use the present perfect.

sections.title: Rule 3: Present simple for facts and for the chart itself
sections.label: Rule 3: Present simple for facts and for the chart itself

paragraphs: The present simple is used for things that are generally true, for habits and for how things normally work. In Task 2, most of your arguments are general statements, so the present simple is your main tense.
In Task 1, the chart exists now, so introduce it in the present simple: The graph shows…, The table compares…. The data inside it may be in the past, but the chart itself is in front of you.

items.text: The bar chart compares the number of students in three countries.
Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
Most people in big cities use public transport every day.

sections.title: Rule 4: Past perfect for “earlier than that”
sections.label: Rule 4: Past perfect for “earlier than that”

paragraphs: Sometimes you need to show that one past event was already complete before another past event. The past perfect (had + past participle) does this job. It is like saying “earlier than that”.
Look for clues such as by the time, already and before. In Task 1, by + a past year often signals the past perfect: By 2010, the figure had doubled.

rows: …by the time the factory closed in 2012.

items.text: When the new policy started, unemployment already fell.
When the new policy started, unemployment had already fallen.
By 2010, the population had doubled.

paragraphs: Some Task 1 charts include future years, such as 2030 or 2050. These figures are predictions, not facts, so you need future forms. Will is correct, but academic writing often uses more cautious phrases that show the figure is only an estimate.
After be expected to, be predicted to and be projected to, the verb is always in its base form: is expected to rise, never is expected to rising.

rows: The population will reach 9 million by 2040.
is predicted / projected to + base verb
The figure is projected to fall to 20%.

items.text: The number is expected to rising after 2030.
The number is expected to rise after 2030.

sections.title: Rule 6: No will after if and when
sections.label: Rule 6: No will after if and when

paragraphs: When you talk about a possible future event after if, unless or when, English uses the present simple, not will. The will goes in the other half of the sentence, the result.
This pattern is very common in Task 2, where you predict the results of policies: If governments invest in education, the economy will grow.

items.text: If the government will raise taxes, people will spend less.
If the government raises taxes, people will spend less.
When the new line will open, traffic will improve.
When the new line opens, traffic will improve.

sections.title: Rule 7: State verbs are not used in the -ing form
sections.label: Rule 7: State verbs are not used in the -ing form

paragraphs: Some verbs describe states rather than actions: what we know, believe, own, want or prefer. These verbs are normally not used in the continuous (-ing) form, even when we are talking about right now.
This matters in Task 2, where you often write about opinions. Many people believe is correct; many people are believing is not.

items.text: Many people are believing that cities are unsafe.
Many people believe that cities are unsafe.
Most students are preferring online classes.
Most students prefer online classes.

paragraphs: Once you choose a time frame for a paragraph, stay in it unless the meaning changes. Jumping between past and present without a reason confuses the reader and makes your writing look careless.

In Task 1, describe all past data in the past simple and switch only for a reason, such as moving to a future projection. In Task 2, keep general arguments in the present simple and use past tenses only for specific past examples.

items.text: In 2005, coal was the main fuel, but in 2015 gas becomes the main fuel.
In 2005, coal was the main fuel, but in 2015 gas became the main fuel.

sections.title: Rule 9: Learn the irregular verbs of Task 1
sections.label: Rule 9: Learn the irregular verbs of Task 1

paragraphs: Many common verbs do not form the past with -ed. They have their own past simple and past participle forms, which simply need to be memorized. Several of them appear in almost every Task 1 report, so a mistake here is very visible.
The verbs below are the ones you are most likely to need when describing trends and changes.

items.text: Prices have rose since 2015.
Prices have risen since 2015.
Sales falled in 2020.
Sales fell in 2020.

paragraphs: Here is how tense choice appears in real IELTS writing. Notice how the time phrase in each sentence decides the tense.

rows: The graph shows car sales in three countries.
The figure is expected to reach 40% by 2040.
Technology has changed the way we work.
Many people believe that exams cause stress.
If cities build more parks, people will be healthier.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common tense mistakes in IELTS essays.
Use this routine for every sentence that contains a time phrase.

steps: Find the time word: in 2010, ago, since, recently, by the time, by 2030.
Match it: finished time → past simple; since / for / recently → present perfect; earlier past → past perfect; future year → will / is expected to.
Check the verb form, especially irregular verbs (rose, risen, fell, fallen).

furtherStudy.description: A chart of every tense with its form and use.

cards.why: In 2015 is a finished time, so we use the past simple.
Since 2020 connects the past with now, so we use the present perfect.

cards.front: The bar chart ____ the number of students in four countries.
cards.why: We introduce a chart in the present simple. Show is not normally used in the -ing form here.

cards.front: By the time the rain stopped, the river ____ its banks.
cards.why: The river burst its banks before the rain stopped, so the earlier event takes the past perfect.

cards.front: The population is expected to ____ ten million by 2040.
cards.why: After is expected to, we always use the base form of the verb.

cards.front: Most experts ____ that the climate is changing.
cards.why: Believe is a state verb, so it is not used in the -ing form.

cards.front: Ten years ago, very few families ____ a car.
cards.why: Ago refers to a finished time, so we use the past simple.
After have, we need the past participle. Rise → rose → risen.

cards.front: If the government ____ taxes, people will spend less.
cards.why: After if, we use the present simple for a future idea. Will goes in the result.

cards.front: I ____ in Sylhet for five years, and I still live here.
cards.why: The action started in the past and continues now, so we use the present perfect.
